Open period, measured up to this moment.
Not counted as downtime (curtailment, low wind…)

Terms, scope, notice deadline under the contract…

This source record has already been imported — re-importing must not create a duplicate.
Alarm code or record id in the source system. Used so that re-importing creates no duplicates.
Set it and the system warns when equipment of the wrong category is installed at this location.
Empty means still installed. Do not invent a removal date for equipment that is still in the machine.
Child periods point back to this one. Unit-hour reports must EXCLUDE this row to avoid double counting.
An outage happens at a PLACE. Which equipment was there is derived from the installation history.
Template "%s" does not say which equipment category it applies to — there is no way to know which locations to generate.
Empty means STILL DOWN. Do not invent an end date for an outage that has not been resolved.
Location "%(vt)s" accepts category "%(mong)s", but asset "%(ts)s" belongs to category "%(co)s".
This location path already exists — two child locations under the same parent cannot share a code.
Derived from the location and the start time. Editable when a different component has to be named explicitly.
knock-on units. Unit-hour reports\n                        must exclude this row to avoid double counting.
An opening suggestion. REAL responsibility is decided by the contract terms, and every contract differs.
This is the field that earns money. Without it an outage is only a log entry; with it, it is a claim you can make.
Leave empty and it sits directly under the equipment. Set it and a multi-level tree is generated — for example three blades inside the rotor.
Which equipment category this template describes the internals of. Usually a root category — for example "Wind turbine".
The LOWER number wins. When two categories occur at the same time on the same equipment, those hours count against the lower-numbered one.
Empty means any category is accepted. Set it and the system warns when equipment of the wrong category is installed here.
A component sits INSIDE another asset and travels with it when removed. Unlike a functional location — the place stays put.
Components removed for overhaul and refitted afterwards, keeping their serial-number history. Suggested value when creating a new asset.
Free-text reference to the handover source. The handover bridge replaces this field with a real link to the contract and the BOQ line.
Every category tree needs an "Other" bucket. Without one, whoever enters data forces records into the nearest category and ruins the statistics.
Loss of the monitoring link. It has to be accounted for as a time category — neither skipped nor treated as a healthy machine.
Equipment locations and component locations hold exactly ONE asset at a time. Plants and systems hold several.
Outage "%s" has no responsibility attributed. Confirm it with this field empty and it stays that way for good — and this is precisely the field that earns money.
OEM contractors usually claim the right to fit refurbished parts. Without recording it, in a few years nobody knows what is actually inside the machine.
.\n                        To move it, record a new installation — do not edit\n                        by hand, because editing by hand loses the history.
The core only builds an empty tree. The domain content — for example the 11\n               subsystems and 19 assemblies of a wind turbine — is loaded by the industry package.
Holds the things removed for overhaul and refitted afterwards — gearbox, generator, blades, converter. These are the locations where serial-number history is worth the most.
Removed, overhauled, then refitted — keeping the serial-number history intact. Gearbox, generator, blades and converter are of this kind. Quite different from consumables.
Same location, same moment, two different time categories. NOT an error — the standard provides a category priority mechanism. But a person has to arbitrate; do not let the machine choose.
Other names for this same category, comma separated. Use it when importing from an OEM or contractor source that uses different words — it stops two categories meaning the same thing being created.
Derived from the failure history of THIS fleet, not from a generic ranking. Data from several sources shows this order differs widely from fleet to fleet.
This location holds one asset at a time.\n To replace the equipment you have to close the old period before\n opening a new one.
A location is a place, not a thing. A location code never\n changes when the equipment is replaced — that is why this table is\n separate from the asset table.

CANNOT be derived from the name. Curtailment under grid constraints is classified as OPERATING (partial output, derated) — not downtime. Get this field wrong and the whole availability figure is wrong.

A step-up substation fault stops the whole fleet: record one outage at the substation, then point each turbine's outage at it. Reports add up the CHILD periods, not the parent — adding both is double counting.

Rated capacity of the unit installed at this location. Used to compute the capacity factor — while it is not declared the system does NOT guess, because dividing by a guessed number gives a plausible-looking ratio that is wrong.

Empty means it is your own. Set it when a removed component belongs to the contractor under a service agreement — this is a clause that has to be negotiated, and without recording it the asset is lost track of.

The day boundary of every daily report follows this time zone. Leave it empty and the company time zone is used, then Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh — but stating it explicitly is better, especially with plants outside Vietnam.
Whether a category is equipment or a component is your own decision:\n open Configuration ▸ Component categories and tick “Is equipment”.\n The system does not infer it.

Mandatory and optional classification under the standard. The availability figure depends on whether the OPTIONAL categories are collected — so compliance with the standard cannot be claimed merely by naming an indicator.
This category does not count as downtime. The textbook\n example is curtailment under grid constraints — the machine is\n still operating, just at partial output.
An asset is a thing, carrying its own history through every\n removal and refit. The location it currently sits in is a temporary\n attribute, derived from the installation history.
Per an APPROVED model — wind conditions and power curve, or a reference turbine. Do NOT take rated power times downtime hours: that is the commonest mis-statement in wind reports.

The same assembly carries different names depending on the source.\n                            Without aliases, importing from two OEMs creates two\n                            categories meaning the same thing, and the statistics add up wrongly.
Each outage is a span of time during which one location is in one\n state. The Responsibility field is the one that earns money:\n without it, an outage is only a log entry.
Click the × on the “Main equipment only” chip in the search\n bar and you see everything. If it is still empty after that, there really\n is no data — check the selections in the left-hand panel.

%(nhan)s "%(ten)s" already has an installation period overlapping this one: %(tu)s → %(den)s.\n\nTwo periods must not overlap. To replace equipment you have to CLOSE the old period (fill in the removal date) before opening the new one — otherwise the history becomes wrong and nobody notices.

Asset "%(con)s" installed at %(vtc)s must sit inside assembly "%(dung)s" (at %(vtd)s), not "%(cha)s".\n\nSkipping a level puts the child at the SAME level as the assembly that contains it — the location tree says one thing, the assembly tree another, and anyone looking sees it at once.

This screen opens with the “Main equipment only” filter on — it shows equipment and hides the components inside them (blades, support frames, bushings, relays…). The category you just picked may contain nothing but components, which is why the list is empty.

Same location, same moment, an outage of another category. Not an error — a machine can be faulty and curtailed at once. But a person has to arbitrate which category those hours count against; do not let the machine choose.

The assembly tree follows the THING, unlike the functional location tree, which stays with the PLACE. Remove a gearbox for overhaul and the bearings inside travel with it. The two trees answer two different questions: "how many times has this location lost a gearbox" (foundation, wind flow, installation faults) and "in how many locations has this gearbox failed" (batch faults).

Downtime known in advance and schedulable: planned maintenance, planned repair work. Distinct from fault downtime — both are downtime hours, but one is inside the plan and the other is not, and the field map colours them differently.\n\nCANNOT be derived from the name. The map used to look for the word "planned" in the category name: the name is a TRANSLATABLE field, so anyone reading the screen in English saw "Planned maintenance" — no string match — and a machine under maintenance showed RED as though it were faulty. A category named "Periodic maintenance" fell into the same hole.

The template generates the functional LOCATION tree — the PLACE, which exists for the life of the plant. However many times the gearbox is replaced, the place stays the same. History anchored here answers "how many times has this location lost a gearbox" — the question that points to foundation, wind-flow or installation faults.
Different from the asset assembly tree (the "Installed in asset" field), which answers the opposite question: "in how many locations has this gearbox failed" — the question that points to batch faults.

Turn this on when the category is a piece of EQUIPMENT — something with a record of its own, its own work orders, its own spare parts, and worth a line of its own in the asset register. Turn it off when it is a COMPONENT sitting inside another piece of equipment.

This flag decides the "Asset level" column of every asset in the category, and decides whether that asset shows up when the Asset register is opened. It is a BUSINESS decision, so it lives here for users to change rather than being inferred from the data.

The system used to infer it: any asset not installed inside another asset was equipment. That inference was wrong — string combiner boxes sit inside PV arrays and turbine inverters sit inside the electrical assembly; both are real equipment, and both vanished from the register.
